entities.name: Boniface I
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Boniface I, who served as Bishop of Rome from December 28, 418 CE, until his death on September 4, 422 CE, navigated one of the most tumultuous periods for the early papacy, marked by a contested election and the assertion of Roman primacy amidst the waning authority of the Western Roman Empire. His papacy is primarily defined by the schism with the antipope Eulalius, a conflict that necessitated imperial intervention and set precedents for the role of secular power in ecclesiastical affairs. Boniface, a Roman by birth, emerged as a pivotal figure in solidifying the administrative and spiritual authority of the Roman See at a critical juncture in Late Antiquity.

The core of Boniface's pontificate was the bitter dispute over his election. Following the death of Pope Zosimus, a faction of the Roman clergy and populace elected the archdeacon Eulalius, while another, larger group simultaneously elected Boniface. Both were consecrated on December 28, 418 CE, leading to a schism that split the Roman Church. Emperor Honorius, residing in Ravenna, initially ordered both claimants to leave Rome but ultimately sided with Boniface after Eulalius defiantly returned, confirming Boniface as the legitimate pope on April 3, 419 CE. During his brief but impactful tenure, Boniface also actively asserted Roman jurisdiction over the churches of Illyricum, clashing with the Eastern Emperor Theodosius II and the Patriarch of Constantinople, further defining the boundaries of papal authority in the East and West.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Boniface I's papacy was critical in consolidating papal authority during a period of schism and imperial decline, setting precedents for church-state relations and reinforcing Roman jurisdictional claims over regions like Illyricum, which profoundly shaped the early medieval Church.
